years_rule: years ~= (8 / ln 2) * ln(HR_now / HR_target); adult mortality doubles about every 8 years (Gompertz)

steps.note: Quartile medians vs the lowest quartile; log-interpolated between medians, flat outside. Plateau age-dependent (lower for 60+).

source.cite: Paluch AE et al. Daily steps and all-cause mortality: a meta-analysis of 15 international cohorts. Lancet Public Health 2022;7(3):e219-e228
source.design: meta-analysis of 15 prospective cohorts, device-measured steps

fitness.note: Per 1 MET higher maximal aerobic capacity (about 1 km/h faster running). Input is the change, not the level.

source.cite: Kodama S et al. Cardiorespiratory fitness as a quantitative predictor of all-cause mortality and cardiovascular events in healthy men and women: a meta-analysis. JAMA 2009;301(19):2024-2035

fruitveg.note: Benefit observed up to 800 g/day; strongest up to ~400 g/day, slight further reduction beyond.

source.cite: Aune D et al. Fruit and vegetable intake and the risk of cardiovascular disease, total cancer and all-cause mortality. Int J Epidemiol 2017;46(3):1029-1056
source.design: systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis, 95 studies (15 for all-cause, combined fruit+veg)

nuts.note: Per 28 g/day; not extrapolated beyond 28 g. Heterogeneity I2 = 66%.

source.cite: Aune D et al. Nut consumption and risk of cardiovascular disease, total cancer, all-cause and cause-specific mortality. BMC Med 2016;14:207
source.design: systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis, 15 studies for all-cause

bmi.note: Per 5 units above 25, approximately log-linear; reference BMI 22.5-25. 22.5-25 treated as reference; below 22.5 risk rises again and is not modelled (rejected).

source.cite: Global BMI Mortality Collaboration. Body-mass index and all-cause mortality: individual-participant-data meta-analysis of 239 prospective studies in four continents. Lancet 2016;388:776-786

sleep.note: Short sleep modelled as <= 6 h (an approximation: the pooled studies used cut-offs from <= 5 to < 7 h), otherwise reference (HR 1). Long sleep (>= 9 h, HR 1.30) is mainly a marker of ill health, so it is recorded but not used: inputs above 8.5 h are rejected (long-sleep cut-offs in the pooled studies started at > 8 h).

source.cite: Cappuccio FP et al. Sleep duration and all-cause mortality: a systematic review and meta-analysis of prospective studies. Sleep 2010;33(5):585-592
source.design: meta-analysis of 16 studies (27 cohorts), 1.38 million participants

verified: 2026-11-02: HRs and CIs checked against abstracts/full texts via web search; DOIs resolved via Crossref
